Nov 16 : The global banking industry is set to enter the next year on a strong footing, reflecting supportive economic conditions and solid profitability, according to a Moody's Ratings report on Monday. The ratings agency said banks have adapted to shifting market conditions and weathered sudden shocks through a rapid monetary tightening cycle, leaving them better prepared to navigate persistent geopolitical and economic uncertainty. Here are more details: • Moody's has a "stable" outlook on global banks for 2027, reflecting its view of credit fundamentals in the sector over the next 12 months

• Economic growth and the unemployment rate are expected to remain stable in the G20 countries as inflation moderates, the report said • Moody's expects geopolitical risks, regulatory easing, private markets growth, long-dated government bond yields, delayed impact of a surge in borrowing costs, and AI and technology investments to shape bank credit quality next year • "The main risk to banks' asset quality is the delayed effect of the 2022-24 tightening cycle and its recent pickup during 2026. Corporate and household borrowers still need to refinance or amortise debt originated in a much lower interest-rate environment," Moody's said • Moody's expects stable interest rates in the second half of 2027 to improve borrowers' refinancing prospects and contain credit losses, although inflationary pressures and corporate refinancing will be the main risk to asset quality

FAST

BERLIN, Nov 16 : As Europe's defence ministries look to limit dependency on American technology and major software company Palantir Technologies for critical military functions, a growing number of firms within the region are competing for their business.  Last week, Germany’s Helsing unveiled military intelligence software called Clarity. It is part of a broader market for AI-powered systems designed to accelerate military decision-making by helping sift through vast quantities of data to help identify threats and recommend action, including targeting and attacks. But Europe currently lacks an exact equivalent that matches Palantir’s scale, deployment footprint and operational experience, some government and military officials say.  That gives European militaries a dilemma: pursue homegrown systems that promise greater autonomy but may be less mature, or rely on a proven platform despite concerns about long-term strategic dependence.

The Trump administration has pushed Europe to take on much greater responsibility for its own security as Washington scales back its military presence in the region, and has placed pressure on the transatlantic NATO alliance.  European officials face similar trade-offs between autonomy and capability across a range of military capabilities, including in the area of satellite communications, which is dominated by Elon Musk’s US company SpaceX.  Ukraine last week reported further significant disruptions of its access to SpaceX, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. France, a vocal advocate for European autonomy, is developing a sovereign AI-enabled military platform called Arcadia. Alexandre Lahousse, the deputy head of France’s defence procurement agency, told Reuters it would include multiple suppliers. The agency plans to award at least some contracts by year’s end and to have an operational version available for field deployment by mid-2027, he said.  Germany, which is also aiming to deploy an AI-based military data integration platform from next year, is weighing domestic and other European options. It has narrowed down a shortlist to a handful of solutions, which does not include Palantir, a person familiar with the matter said. The person said the solutions under consideration would not match Palantir's capabilities but would be good enough, ensure national data sovereignty and should be able to achieve about 80 per cent of what is needed within a year. The Netherlands currently uses some Palantir software but says it wants a European alternative within two years. The Dutch military is meeting potential suppliers and will likely require a combination of Dutch and other European providers, Dutch arms procurement minister Derk Boswijk told Reuters. "We have a lot of knowledge in Europe when it comes to AI and decision-making. But it's very fragmented, and that is the problem," Boswijk said. NATO'S MAVEN ROLL OUT Palantir’s Maven Smart System has been widely used by Ukraine in its fight against Russia while the Pentagon has adopted it as its core military software and has used it in its war with Iran this year.  “I've yet to find anything that can pull together as much of a diverse set of data and allow us the ability to make sense of that data as flexibly,” NATO's top commander, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, told Reuters this summer.  NATO’s military headquarters adopted Palantir's Maven Smart System last year and said in June that it was ready for routine alliance-wide operational use.  Militaries are wrestling with many questions, including around data security, who trains the AI systems, and ensuring different platforms work seamlessly together, said Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, Germany's army chief, at a conference in Berlin on Friday.  “There’s the issue of interoperability when we fight in alliances — and we always fight in alliances.” NATO officials have previously warned of an increased threat from Russia, which they say could potentially mount a large-scale assault on allied territory as early as 2029. Moscow denies aggressive intentions. Helsing said it could supply an initial version of its Clarity software within a matter of months to the German military’s Lithuania brigade, widely viewed as the Bundeswehr unit most likely to see frontline combat in the event of a conflict with Russia. Other European makers of military software include Denmark’s Systematic, whose SitaWare product is used by the Bundeswehr and parts of NATO, as well as traditional defence companies like France’s Thales and Safran, plus startups such as Paris-based Comand AI. For its part, Palantir has sought to reassure Europeans that its military AI system used by NATO has no "kill switch." Palantir's international chief Louis Mosley told Reuters there remains demand in Europe for its products including in the UK, where the defence ministry last year signed a three-year enterprise agreement with the US company.  Mosley added he still hopes to persuade Germany to adopt Palantir’s software with the pitch that it has battlefield-tested capability that works today.

(Sabine Siebold in Berlin, Florence Loeve in Paris, Cassell Bryan-Low in London and Andrew Gray in Brussels; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

Source: Reuters

FAST

Nov 16 : Blackstone-backed Mphasis said companies globally are increasing cybersecurity spending in the race to strengthen their defences, CEO Nitin Rakesh told Reuters, as AI enables increasingly sophisticated attacks that are faster and cheaper. Banks and insurers are leading the increase in cybersecurity spending, aided by larger technology budgets and regulatory requirements, while retailers and consumer firms are also stepping up investments to protect customer data, Rakesh said last week, without providing figures. The comments follow a record $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, in which hackers used social engineering and compromised AI tools, highlighting the growing complexity of cyber threats. Against that backdrop, companies are stepping up cybersecurity spending as AI makes attacks faster and cheaper and increases the number of vulnerabilities they must address.

IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach report underscored the trend, finding AI-driven attacks rose 56 per cent from a year earlier, while the global average cost of a data breach climbed 12 per cent to nearly $5 million. A related survey found awareness of advanced AI cyber threats prompted 85 per cent of organisations to plan higher security spending, versus 64 per cent after suffering a breach. Rakesh said clients were increasingly investing in identity and access controls covering employees, software accounts and automated agents, while also using AI to detect and fix vulnerabilities. While threat detection is already heavily automated, fixing vulnerabilities still requires significant manual work, he said. "You can't really throw people at that problem because you won't be able to keep up with the volume that is required in the time-frame that you need to fix those patches," Rakesh said.

TOKYO: The Bank of Japan must raise its policy rate to a "good" position at an early stage and focus on forestalling upside price risks including from the Middle East conflict, its board member Hajime Takata said on Monday (Nov 16). "I believe the bank needs to conduct rate hikes nimbly after gauging the degree of accommodation in domestic financial conditions, in addition to examining developments overseas," he said in a speech. The BOJ kept interest rates steady at 1.25 per cent last month but declared victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target and stressed its policy has entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot, reinforcing its hawkish bias. Takata, who proposed unsuccessfully to raise interest rates to 1.5 per cent last month, said inflationary pressures could intensify in the latter half of the current fiscal year that ends in March 2027 and push inflation above the BOJ's 2 per cent target.

"The BOJ must thus shift its stance away from encouraging a rise in underlying inflation, towards demonstrating to markets its determination to prevent upward deviations in prices," he said. With underlying inflation having reached 2 per cent, the BOJ must move its policy rate sufficiently close to levels deemed neutral to the economy, Takata said. BOJ staff calculations place Japan's nominal neutral rate, which neither heats up nor slows the economy, at between 1.1 per cent and 2.5 per cent, offering a rough guide on how far policymakers could lift borrowing costs. "It's necessary to place the BOJ's policy rate at an early stage in what I would call a 'good' position - that is, a level near the median of the estimated neutral rate range," Takata said.

FAST

PERTH, Nov 16 : Oil prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus as shipments from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz have been nearly restored to pre-war levels and the US took steps to support moving fuel cargoes between domestic ports. Brent futures were down 47 cents, or 0.49 per cent, to $95.37 a barrel by 0145 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 23 cents, or 0.26 per cent, to $88.33. Oil closed lower on Friday as the market weighed signs of lowering geopolitical risk from the US-Israeli war against Iran, now in its ninth month. The benchmarks fell 16 per cent and 13 per cent, respectively, the prior week. The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.

"For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness. That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members' emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Prices were also pressured down by the US decision to extend a waiver of a shipping law that will continue to allow foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and fuels such as gasoline and diesel more easily between US ports. US President Donald Trump extended for 90 days a waiver of the Jones Act, which requires US-flagged ships to carry cargo between US ports, a White House official said on Friday. Waiving the rule opens up the number of tankers available to carry commodities between US ports.  Still, Waterer noted that while supply was loosening, shipping rates remained high, putting a floor on oil prices. Rates remain high because of the risks the tankers face carrying crude through the Strait of Hormuz and because the number of ships tied up in shuttling oil through the waterway for transfer to other ships that take shipments to refineries has reduced the vessel supply. On Sunday night, Iran's navy said that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 16 : Asian shares fell on Monday after a whiplash week capped by the shock exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, with the chipmaker's earnings and Anthropic's IPO this week set to test whether the AI-fuelled bull market still has further to run. Also later in the week, US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen to discuss nuclear arms reduction and the US-Israeli war with Iran. The minutes of the US Federal Reserve's October policy meeting are due on Wednesday, while a parade of Fed speakers will also be on the bill this week. Markets will be alert for any hint of policymakers being receptive to the idea of an outsized 50-basis-point interest rate hike next month. In Asia on Monday, Japan's Nikkei fell 0.6 per cent, while South Korea slipped 0.2 per cent. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.

S&P 500 futures edged up 0.3 per cent, while Nasdaq futures bounced 0.5 per cent. Nvidia, the poster child of a four-year US bull market, has seen its market value tumble from about $5.8 trillion in early October to $3.9 trillion as of Friday, LSEG data showed, as investors rushed for the exit after Huang's departure. Analysts expect earnings growth of 90 per cent on revenue of $109 billion in Nvidia's fiscal third quarter when its earnings are due on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with all eyes on whether the chipmaker will stick to its bullish outlook for next year under new management. "Options markets imply an earnings-day move of approximately +/-7 per cent, yet I question whether the quarterly numbers will carry their usual significance," said Chris Weston, head of research at foreign exchange brokerage Pepperstone. "Nvidia may well deliver another exceptional beat and raise at tomorrow's earnings, but investors are increasingly trying to value a business in FY2028 and FY2029 potentially without the individual who architected its competitive advantage." The Financial Times reported Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning as CEO. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs to "go outside the company" for a new CEO. Just two days after Nvidia's earnings, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is scheduled to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade. The firm's IPO has drawn more institutional interest than SpaceX, people familiar with the matter told Reuters. US DOLLAR LIFTS WITH YIELDS Data on Friday showed US producer prices rose in October a touch less than markets had expected, though there were signs that inflation pressure was broadening. Together with a hotter-than-forecast consumer price index report, Friday's figures led analysts to estimate a 0.3 per cent rise in core personal consumption expenditure for October, which would be the third successive monthly increase at that pace. The PCE index is the Fed's preferred gauge of inflation when considering whether to change its policy interest rate. Fed funds futures imply a quarter-point rate hike next month is essentially locked in, while odds for a 50-basis-point move lengthened to 6 per cent from 12 per cent a day earlier. A total tightening of 90 basis points is priced in by late next year. In San Francisco on Monday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is set to tell a public forum that artificial intelligence will reshape the US economy, but how the region's new tech boom evolves, and on what timetable, is a wild card for central bankers. In government debt, US Treasuries were steady after rate-hike expectations prompted their biggest weekly fall since April last year, when the trigger was Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs. Two-year yields were little changed at 4.8652 per cent after surging 35 basis points last week. Ten-year yields were flat at 5.1433 per cent, having jumped 29 bps to be back above the psychologically important 5 per cent level. The US dollar lifted with yield support, rising 1.1 per cent last week against major peers to its highest since April last year. The dollar index was steady at 103.42 on Monday. In commodities, oil prices were mostly steady after two weeks of decline. Brent futures fell 0.2 per cent to $95.69 a barrel, having dropped 2.5 per cent last week, while US crude futures edged 0.1 per cent higher to $88.68, after falling by a similar amount last week. Non-interest-bearing gold bounced 0.3 per cent to $3,891 an ounce, having fallen 4.6 per cent last week.

Source: Reuters

Japan's economy unexpectedly shrinks as inflation squeezes households

The first contraction in four quarters underscores the uneven nature of Japan's economic recovery, with households remaining vulnerable to persistent inflation despite rising wages.

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 16 : Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in the July-September quarter, reflecting weak consumer spending as higher living costs forced households to tighten their budgets. Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1 per cent quarter-on-quarter, official data showed on Monday, compared with a median market forecast of 0.3 per cent annualised growth in a Reuters poll, and a revised 1.7 per cent expansion in the previous quarter. The decline is the first in four quarters and underscores the uneven nature of Japan's economic recovery, with households remaining vulnerable to persistent inflation despite rising wages. Still, policymakers are unlikely to view the weakness as a brake on Japan's moderate recovery, with resilient corporate activity, rising real wages and robust demand for artificial intelligence-related investment underpinning growth.

"While growth was indeed negative this time, there is no need to be overly pessimistic about the result," said Kento Minami, senior economist at Daiwa Securities. "My impression is that moderate growth is probably continuing." Minami also said the results are unlikely to derail the Bank of Japan's tightening path, as the central bank remains focused on inflation risks, adding that firm domestic price pressures and a global backdrop of higher interest rates leave little room for a dovish policy shift. The reading translated into a quarterly fall of 0.02 per cent, compared with the median estimate of a 0.1 per cent increase. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of economic output, fell 0.3 per cent, compared with a market estimate of a 0.2 per cent decline. Persistent price pressures and poor weather, including heavy rain and typhoons during the quarter, hurt household spending. Demand for automobiles and air conditioners retreated following the temporary boost in the previous quarter from tax and regulatory changes. "Strong wage growth should support consumption, but higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will continue to squeeze household purchasing power," said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, rose 1.6 per cent, versus a market forecast for a 1.5 per cent increase, backed by investment in labour-saving technologies and AI-related projects. Net external demand, or exports minus imports, knocked 0.6 per centage point off growth, compared with a market forecast for a 0.4 per centage point drag on GDP growth. Imports rose sharply as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified procurement following disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East. "Looking ahead, improvements in the employment and income environment, as well as the effects of various policy measures, are expected to support a gradual recovery in the economy," Japanese economy minister Minoru Kiuchi said in a statement. "However, it will be necessary to continue closely monitoring the impact of the Middle East situation," he said. BOJ RATE-HIKE PATH The BOJ will closely scrutinise the latest data as it assesses whether the economy can withstand further interest-rate increases. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ has stepped up its policy tightening this year, delivering interest rate hikes in June and September. Many analysts expect the next BOJ rate hike as soon as December. "While consumption remained weak, that was largely a consequence of rising prices," reinforcing the need for the BOJ to keep raising interest rates, said Kazutaka Maeda, senior economist at Meiji Yasuda Research Institute. But Ryosuke Katagi, a market economist at Mizuho Securities, said in a note to clients that if weakness in consumer spending persists, it could sharpen differences among BOJ board members, as dovish policymakers cite fragile private consumption as a reason to proceed cautiously with further rate hikes. A monthly survey of 37 economists by the Japan Center for Economic Research showed the economy is expected to grow 0.89 per cent in fiscal 2026 and 1.02 per cent in fiscal 2027, suggesting economists see growth remaining modest but resilient. Japan's longer-term growth challenges remain in focus, with the International Monetary Fund projecting the country will slip to the world's sixth-largest economy in nominal dollar terms in 2027 in dollar terms, overtaken by India and Britain. Japan is currently the world's fourth-largest after Germany.

SEOUL: South Korea's SK Hynix said on Monday (Nov 16) it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won (US$1.05 billion) over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, aiming to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market. The chipmaker also outlined plans for a jointly funded 874.6 billion won testing facility at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul, where smaller suppliers will be able to test products under conditions similar to those on commercial chip production lines. SK Hynix said its supplier support programme covers four stages - research and development, testing, mass production and sales. It aims to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology hurdles. The testing facility, named Trinity Fab, is a partnership between SK Hynix, the central government and local governments. It is scheduled to open in May 2027. SK Hynix will contribute 443.2 billion won, the central government 373.6 billion won and local governments 57.7 billion won, according to the company.

The facility will be housed within the first chip plant at SK Hynix's Yongin semiconductor cluster, 40km south of Seoul, where the company plans to invest 600 trillion won to build four chip fabrication plants. It will include a 3,305 sq m cleanroom and equipment for processes including lithography, etching, deposition and inspection. Suppliers will be able to evaluate materials and equipment using 12-inch wafers before deploying them on production lines. SK Hynix said the shared facility would help small suppliers reduce testing costs and shorten the time needed to bring products to market. It will be run by an independent non-profit foundation to protect intellectual property and commercially sensitive information. Under its research support programme, SK Hynix will provide up to 50 per cent of initial development costs in advance and compensate suppliers for work undertaken even if a project fails to meet its targets. Intel has been sued by shareholders who accused the US chipmaker of defrauding them by concealing the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales that caused its stock price to plunge nearly 29 per cent in a single day. In a proposed class action filed on Friday (Nov 13) in the San Jose, California, federal court, shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund said Intel was too slow to disclose information about how slowing PC sales and an inventory glut would weigh on revenue. The shareholders said Intel's problems with PC sales and excess inventory outweighed data centre construction and other benefits related to the artificial intelligence boom. They also said Intel had the motive and opportunity to defraud by raising capital in mid-August, halfway through its "disastrous" third quarter, when it sold US$23 billion of stock at US$95 per share.

The sale came as Intel looked to build out its chip contract manufacturing business, a key part of Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan's business strategy. Shares of Intel closed Friday at US$59.66. Intel did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sunday. Shares of Intel fell 28.6 per cent on Oct 30, wiping out about US$140 billion of market value, one day after the Santa Clara, California-based company projected lower-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue and profit and forecast a prolonged slowdown in PC sales. Tan told analysts that he was disappointed by manufacturing supply shortages, an "unprecedented memory crunch," and resulting softness in PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan added. Like many other large technology companies, Intel has poured money into manufacturing, but supply disruptions have made it harder to benefit from growing demand for data centre chips. Meanwhile, rising memory prices have made PCs more expensive, weighing on demand. Friday's lawsuit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, seeks unspecified damages for Intel shareholders between Jul 23, 2026, and Oct 29, 2026. Tan and Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner are also defendants. Intel shares are up 62 per cent this year through Friday, though they have slid from their recent peak of US$142.35 on Jun 30.

BROWNSVILLE, Texas, Nov 15 : A Vulcan rocket owned by United Launch Alliance, the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed on Sunday shortly after liftoff from Florida, destroying its payload of 40 satellites for Amazon's Leo internet network in the launch company's first mission failure. The rocket failed roughly 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, and the cause was not immediately clear. It represented a major setback for the two-decade-old company's new flagship rocket as it sought to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet constellation. "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement. "Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."

The mission was Vulcan's fifth since its 2024 debut and first in nine months, following a launch hiatus drawn out by separate technical investigations into its solid rocket side-boosters and its core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin space company. The boosters were being scrutinized for issues encountered on Vulcan's last two flights, including a mission in February for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads to orbit, but the Pentagon had not yet approved the rocket to resume flying national security payloads, pending its performance with the Amazon mission on Sunday. Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket with the BE-4 engine had a launchpad explosion in May, and its investigation determined the engine was the cause. That led the company to modify those delivered to ULA for Vulcan, ULA spokesperson Jessica Rye told Reuters in August. It was unclear if the BE-4 engines played a role in Sunday's mission failure. It appeared to occur after the separation of Vulcan's second stage, the portion carrying the Amazon satellites, from the first-stage booster powered by the BE-4 engines. The failure is another setback for Amazon as it races to deploy satellites using third-party launch providers, many of which have had groundings and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May happened days before it was due to launch Amazon Leo satellites. The rocket failures have persistently held up Amazon's bid to rival SpaceX's vast Starlink internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide. Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been deployed across 14 launches, about 12 per cent of Amazon's plan. The company has hoped to start initial internet service this year.

Controlling shareholder Chow Tai Fook Enterprises (CTFE), which owns about 45.3 per cent of the company, has committed to take up its full entitlement and fully underwrite the remaining shares. The maximum CTFE commitment is about HK$18.7 billion. A CTFE statement said it supports New World Development resuming dividend payments when its financial performance and liquidity permit. The company plans to use about 34 per cent of the proceeds to prepay 10 per cent of about HK$82 billion in bank loans and extend the maturity of the remaining 90 per cent by two years. It plans to use another third to repay debt, including senior notes and deferred distribution of its perpetual securities. After the rights issue, New World's net debt to total equity ratio will drop to 48.3 per cent from 68.3 per cent. The developer aims to reduce total debt by between HK$40 billion and HK$50 billion by the end of 2031 to HK$93 billion to HK$103 billion New World's shares will resume trading on Monday after being suspended on Friday pending the announcement.

STARBASE, Texas: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft on Saturday (Nov 14) returned from a 22-hour voyage in orbit and descended for the first time into the grasp of giant mechanical arms at the Texas tower it was launched from a day earlier, a catch that is essential to the company's decade-long effort to develop a fully reusable rocket. The 52m Starship fell out of thick clouds over SpaceX's Starbase launch site, reignited engines to flip itself vertical and slowly descended into the tower's "Mechazilla" arms, engines still roaring. Charred from the blazing heat of its return from space, the ship shut down its engines and hung still after the rocket system's longest mission yet. "That was the missing link, the holy grail of spaceflight," SpaceX mission commentator Dan Huot said of the ship catch. The towering two-stage rocket's Super Heavy booster - the rocket's bottom half - carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX's Starbase, Texas, facilities. That booster had failed to make a similar return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after liftoff, nixing SpaceX's plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.

But the Starship upper stage's successful return after orbiting Earth 14 times for 22.5 hours marked a key engineering milestone in the whirlwind, multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees as the future workhorse for SpaceX's lucrative Starlink satellite business, as well as ambitions to put data centres in orbit, return humans to the moon and, eventually, settle on Mars.

After deploying 26 Starlink satellites in orbit Friday night while cruising some 260km in altitude, Starship on Saturday fired one of its engines to begin an atmospheric plunge while flying eastward over the Pacific Ocean. It faced blistering heat as its orbital speed of some 17,000 miles per hour slowed to a supersonic free-fall in the skies above SpaceX's Starbase facilities on the Gulf Coast of south Texas. With its aerodynamic fins folded back, two small fittings near the top of Starship hooked onto the launch tower's mechanical arms that had closed in to grasp it, allowing the vessel to hang a few hundred feet off the ground. Musk and SpaceX engineers began inspecting the ship within hours of its catch. "Ship 42 looks great!" Musk wrote on X, posting photos and videos from the launch tower. SHIP'S RETURN ADVANCES ROCKET REUSABILITY SpaceX's dominance in the global launch industry is centred on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which has launched over 700 times since 2010. That rocket's first stage is reusable, but its second stage - the part that delivers payloads into orbit - is discarded into the ocean after each flight. With Starship, Musk wants a rocket system that can fly to space and back in a manner and tempo akin to commercial airplanes, with minimal refurbishment between flights.

SpaceX's mega rocket Starship returns to its launch pad to be caught by the launch tower following a test flight from Starbase, Texas, on Nov 14, 2026. (Photo: AP/Eric Gay)

Though Saturday's Starship recovery is a key milestone in that effort, SpaceX has yet to recover both Starship stages in a single mission, which would mark the first-ever return of an orbital launch system. And Starship's heat shield, composed of hundreds of black hexagonal tiles that protect it from the blazing heat of atmospheric reentry, is itself not yet fully reusable. SpaceX is trying to engineer new tile designs that will require little to no refurbishment after each mission. NASA's Space Shuttle system that ferried astronauts to the International Space Station before its 2011 retirement was partially reusable; its external fuel tanks that got it off Earth were discarded after each flight. The reusable spacecraft itself had to go through extensive refurbishment before re-flying. SpaceX has spent more than US$15 billion on Starship's development. NASA has provided US$3.2 billion as part of a contract valued at more than US$4 billion that SpaceX won in 2021 to return humans to the moon using Starship under the space agency's Artemis program. NASA expects Starship, along with another moon lander under development by Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, to start crewed flights to the moon in 2028, though several challenging development milestones remain with both mooncraft. For Starship, those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable the ship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon.

Source: Reuters/rj/ec
